# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

draft.body:
# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

lines: -I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

+I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk, so I want this memo to start from that uncertainty rather than a conclusion. The pilot week saw 160 boardings in week A and 240 in week B [@lyra:1]. These numbers count trips, not unique people [@lyra:1]. Because boardings track total rides rather than individual students, an increase in count does not prove that more distinct students used the service. The data shows higher usage frequency during the pilot week, but it does not establish a causal link to student attendance. The weeks also differed in academic schedule, and the pilot was not randomized [@lyra:1]. Therefore, the observed increase in boardings reflects higher trip volume, not a guaranteed improvement in classroom presence.

-My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

+The boarding data raises the question of who actually benefits, but the survey data cannot answer it. Eighteen voluntary survey responses came from shuttle riders [@lyra:2]. Non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2]. The responses describe these respondents and cannot establish demand across all students [@lyra:2]. Additionally, no attendance data were collected during the pilot period [@lyra:1]. Without data on non-riders or classroom presence, the survey reflects only the perspectives of existing users. I cannot infer whether students who did not ride the shuttle would have attended class more often if the service had been available to them. The evidence therefore supports further investigation rather than a final judgment on demand or impact.

+Because the pilot currently lacks attendance records and only captures rider perspectives, extending it for one more term offers a chance to test whether the service affects broader engagement, not just the number of boardings observed between the two observation weeks (160 in week A and 240 in week B) [@lyra:1]. This extension should be conditional on collecting better data rather than serving as a celebration of current performance. My goal is not to declare that the shuttle has solved student attendance, a claim the available evidence cannot support. Instead, the continued operation provides a necessary window to measure who can use the service and who remains excluded. The extra term allows the committee to evaluate the pilot’s actual reach before making a permanent decision.

+Because non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2], the current data describe only existing passengers and cannot establish demand across all students. To fix this gap, I propose a short, voluntary questionnaire targeting students who skipped the shuttle, distributed through a general, feasible method that does not assume specific logistics. This approach avoids inventing costs or emissions metrics that were not collected in the initial phase [@lyra:2]. Until we hear from non-riders, any claim about the service’s full impact remains incomplete. I am not suggesting we finalize the pilot’s status based on rider counts alone. The extension should serve as a practical opportunity to gather missing perspectives, ensuring that future decisions rest on a broader picture of student access rather than just the voices of those already riding the bus.

## Evidence

I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk, so I want this memo to start from that uncertainty rather than a conclusion. The pilot week saw 160 boardings in week A and 240 in week B [@lyra:1]. These numbers count trips, not unique people [@lyra:1]. Because boardings track total rides rather than individual students, an increase in count does not prove that more distinct students used the service. The data shows higher usage frequency during the pilot week, but it does not establish a causal link to student attendance. The weeks also differed in academic schedule, and the pilot was not randomized [@lyra:1]. Therefore, the observed increase in boardings reflects higher trip volume, not a guaranteed improvement in classroom presence.

The boarding data raises the question of who actually benefits, but the survey data cannot answer it. Eighteen voluntary survey responses came from shuttle riders [@lyra:2]. Non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2]. The responses describe these respondents and cannot establish demand across all students [@lyra:2]. Additionally, no attendance data were collected during the pilot period [@lyra:1]. Without data on non-riders or classroom presence, the survey reflects only the perspectives of existing users. I cannot infer whether students who did not ride the shuttle would have attended class more often if the service had been available to them. The evidence therefore supports further investigation rather than a final judgment on demand or impact.

## Recommendation

Because the pilot currently lacks attendance records and only captures rider perspectives, extending it for one more term offers a chance to test whether the service affects broader engagement, not just the number of boardings observed between the two observation weeks (160 in week A and 240 in week B) [@lyra:1]. This extension should be conditional on collecting better data rather than serving as a celebration of current performance. My goal is not to declare that the shuttle has solved student attendance, a claim the available evidence cannot support. Instead, the continued operation provides a necessary window to measure who can use the service and who remains excluded. The extra term allows the committee to evaluate the pilot’s actual reach before making a permanent decision.

Because non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2], the current data describe only existing passengers and cannot establish demand across all students. To fix this gap, I propose a short, voluntary questionnaire targeting students who skipped the shuttle, distributed through a general, feasible method that does not assume specific logistics. This approach avoids inventing costs or emissions metrics that were not collected in the initial phase [@lyra:2]. Until we hear from non-riders, any claim about the service’s full impact remains incomplete. I am not suggesting we finalize the pilot’s status based on rider counts alone. The extension should serve as a practical opportunity to gather missing perspectives, ensuring that future decisions rest on a broader picture of student access rather than just the voices of those already riding the bus.

This approach avoids inventing costs or emissions metrics that were not collected in the initial phase [@lyra:2]. Until we hear from non-riders, any claim about the service’s full impact remains incomplete. I am not suggesting we finalize the pilot’s status based on rider counts alone. The extension should serve as a practical opportunity to gather missing perspectives, ensuring that future decisions rest on a broader picture of student access rather than just the voices of those already riding the bus.

live_draft_suggestions.base_content:
# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Evidence
live_draft_blocks.content: I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk, so I want this memo to start from that uncertainty rather than a conclusion. The pilot week saw 160 boardings in week A and 240 in week B [@lyra:1]. These numbers count trips, not unique people [@lyra:1]. Because boardings track total rides rather than individual students, an increase in count does not prove that more distinct students used the service. The data shows higher usage frequency during the pilot week, but it does not establish a causal link to student attendance. The weeks also differed in academic schedule, and the pilot was not randomized [@lyra:1]. Therefore, the observed increase in boardings reflects higher trip volume, not a guaranteed improvement in classroom presence.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Evidence
live_draft_blocks.content: The boarding data raises the question of who actually benefits, but the survey data cannot answer it. Eighteen voluntary survey responses came from shuttle riders [@lyra:2]. Non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2]. The responses describe these respondents and cannot establish demand across all students [@lyra:2]. Additionally, no attendance data were collected during the pilot period [@lyra:1]. Without data on non-riders or classroom presence, the survey reflects only the perspectives of existing users. I cannot infer whether students who did not ride the shuttle would have attended class more often if the service had been available to them. The evidence therefore supports further investigation rather than a final judgment on demand or impact.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Recommendation
live_draft_blocks.content: Because the pilot currently lacks attendance records and only captures rider perspectives, extending it for one more term offers a chance to test whether the service affects broader engagement, not just the number of boardings observed between the two observation weeks (160 in week A and 240 in week B) [@lyra:1]. This extension should be conditional on collecting better data rather than serving as a celebration of current performance. My goal is not to declare that the shuttle has solved student attendance, a claim the available evidence cannot support. Instead, the continued operation provides a necessary window to measure who can use the service and who remains excluded. The extra term allows the committee to evaluate the pilot’s actual reach before making a permanent decision.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Recommendation
live_draft_blocks.content: Because non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2], the current data describe only existing passengers and cannot establish demand across all students. To fix this gap, I propose a short, voluntary questionnaire targeting students who skipped the shuttle, distributed through a general, feasible method that does not assume specific logistics. This approach avoids inventing costs or emissions metrics that were not collected in the initial phase [@lyra:2]. Until we hear from non-riders, any claim about the service’s full impact remains incomplete. I am not suggesting we finalize the pilot’s status based on rider counts alone. The extension should serve as a practical opportunity to gather missing perspectives, ensuring that future decisions rest on a broader picture of student access rather than just the voices of those already riding the bus.
